records.why: Kit list and steps rewritten so that only plant material is handled: Part A (onion slide) is unchanged, Part B uses a photomicrograph instead of a cheek swab. Cotton buds, the second slide and methylene blue were removed from the kit; a millimetre ruler was added for the size estimate.
records.value: Learners work in pairs at benches. Each pair has: 1 glass slide, 1 cover slip, iodine solution in a dropper bottle, a piece of fresh onion (cut into quarters by the teacher beforehand), forceps or a ruler edge, a dropper or small container of clean water, tissue paper, a transparent millimetre ruler, and a light microscope. Each pair also has a printed or projected photomicrograph of human cheek cells stained with methylene blue (from the textbook, the ARES platform, or a prepared slide if the school has one). PART A — Onion Epidermal Cell: Learners peel a thin transparent layer from between two onion scales using forceps (the teacher demonstrates this first). The tissue is placed on a slide with one drop of water, flattened, and a cover slip lowered at an angle to avoid air bubbles. One drop of iodine solution is drawn under the cover slip using tissue paper on the opposite side. Learners focus under low power (4x or 10x objective) then switch to high power (40x objective). They observe and draw what they see in a circle representing the field of view, label what they can identify, and write the magnification used. PART B — Cheek Cell (photomicrograph): Learners study the photomicrograph of human cheek cells, draw one cell and label what they can identify. Learners then complete a structured comparison table: FEATURE | ONION CELL | CHEEK CELL — with rows for shape, cell wall visible (yes/no), nucleus visible (yes/no), colour, other observations.

PART A — Onion Epidermal Cell: Learners peel a thin transparent layer from between two onion scales using forceps (the teacher demonstrates this first). The tissue is placed on a slide with one drop of water, flattened, and a cover slip lowered at an angle to avoid air bubbles. records.why: Normal red blood cells are biconcave; sickle cells are crescent shaped. In sickle cell anaemia a gene change makes abnormal haemoglobin (HbS). When oxygen is low it forms long rods inside the cell, bending it into a stiff crescent. These cells are sticky and rigid, clump and block narrow capillaries, and are destroyed faster than normal cells (days versus about 120 days), causing anaemia and pain. TEACHER KEY (what a good answer sounds like): RED BLOOD CELL — biconcave disc gives a large surface area, no nucleus leaves room for more haemoglobin, and the cell is flexible enough to squeeze through capillaries. GUARD CELL — a pair of bean-shaped cells around a stoma: when they take in water and become turgid they curve apart and the pore opens; when they lose water the pore closes, controlling water loss and gas exchange. ROOT HAIR CELL — a long thin extension greatly increases surface area for absorbing water and mineral ions from the soil. MUSCLE CELL — long fibre that shortens to contract; many mitochondria supply the energy. NERVE CELL — a long axon carries impulses over long distances, dendrites receive signals. SPERM CELL — streamlined head carrying DNA, a flagellum to swim, and a midpiece packed with mitochondria for energy. If a group says 'the shape is just like that', ask: 'What job would that shape help with?' Early finishers may add two more KICD examples: a PALISADE cell (tall, packed with chloroplasts just below the leaf surface to capture light) and a POLLEN grain (tough outer wall protects the male cell on its journey between flowers).

records.why: Audit item confirmed: the old exemplar said the crescent 'disrupts the packing of haemoglobin' and cells 'stack'. The corrected mechanism is the same as Lesson 6 (checked against two sources). The prompt itself is fine: naming the crescent shape is the observation learners are given, and the question asks for the consequences, so that audit comment is a false alarm.
records.old: The crescent cells disrupt the packing of haemoglobin and stack together and block capillaries, so less oxygen is delivered to the body tissues. This causes serious health problems for the affected person, including tiredness and pain. This shows that structure and function are closely linked: a cell is shaped to do a particular job, and even a small structural change caused by a single gene mutation can disrupt that job in measurable, life-affecting ways.
records.new: A change (mutation) in the haemoglobin gene makes abnormal haemoglobin, which forms long rods inside the cell when oxygen is low and bends it into a crescent. The stiff, sticky crescent cells cannot squeeze through narrow capillaries, so they clump and block them, and less oxygen is delivered to the body tissues. They also break down faster than normal cells, so the person becomes anaemic. This causes serious health problems for the affected person, including tiredness and pain. This shows that structure and function are closely linked: a cell is shaped to do a particular job, and even a small structural change caused by a single gene mutation can disrupt that job in measurable, life-affecting ways.
records.reference: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Ch. 18.3 Erythrocytes; US NHLBI, Sickle Cell Disease overview

value.criterion: Shared cell features and cell types
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: names all four universal features (membrane, cytoplasm, DNA, ribosomes), notes that the mature red blood cell is a special case, correctly distinguishes prokaryotes from eukaryotes and uses a full CER with evidence and reasoning.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: names most universal features and states that bacteria are cells, but evidence or reasoning is incomplete.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: names few shared features or confuses what makes something a cell.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: correctly names cell wall, chloroplasts and central vacuole, explains the function of each and links them to the shape and colour of the sukuma wiki cell and to why the onion layer is not green.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: names the plant structures with some functions, with limited links to the observed cells.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: lists structures without functions or mixes up plant and animal features.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: explains clearly how the structure of the red blood cell, white blood cell and another specialised cell suits its job, including the trade-off of losing the nucleus, and places the cell in the levels of organisation from cell to organism.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: links structure to function correctly for most examples but with limited detail.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: states structures or functions separately without linking them.

records.why: The CBE rubric has four levels (Exceeds, Meets, Approaches, Below Expectations) but the data contract allows only three level fields (excellent, proficient, developing) and the printed headings are fixed by the template, so 'Below Expectations' cannot be represented. Suggested: teachers treat any response that does not reach 'Approaches Expectations' as Below Expectations, or the partner contract and template add a fourth field.
